source.title: SPECTRALLY-NORMALIZED MARGIN BOUNDS FOR NEURAL NETWORKS

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is supplied
record.tranche_reason: Empirically measures spectral complexity and margins against excess risk during AlexNet training on natural and randomized data; this is a conceptual test of the measured-property relation in V7, not a test of magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness itself.
record.gate_note: Rows capture the paper's own AlexNet margin-distribution and excess-risk results, plus its explicitly quantified adversarial-noise comparison. The plotted curves have no precise numerical values in the text. The claim versions about memorization capacity, architecture, optimizers, batches, dropout, and memorized-example removal are not tested. Cited results from Zhang et al. are not rows.
record.test_reason: Figure 1 independently compares AlexNet trained with natural and random CIFAR-10 labels using the same unregularized SGD recipe. It marks zero training error and plots test-minus-training error, bearing directly on V1. Spectral complexity and normalized margins do not test V7's magnitude-aware weight-perturbation measure.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors present a spectral-complexity margin bound and find empirical associations with task difficulty, excess risk, and stabilized normalized margins. They suggest that SGD selects complexity appropriate to task difficulty, but leave proving that SGD returns large-margin predictors open. Their experiments show little visible margin benefit from weight decay; they also characterize its generalization impact as small.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains AlexNet with vanilla SGD and examines margins, spectral complexity, and excess risk. It is a conceptual investigation of a related measured property, not the magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation test in V7.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and label condition change the normalized margin distributions; the CIFAR-10 margin distributions converge over training; varying l2 regularization does not visibly improve margins.

fits_no_version.finding: Lipschitz constants distinguish natural- and random-label excess risks, but grow after excess risk plateaus; margin normalization removes that growth.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Margin-normalized spectral complexity can track task difficulty and stabilize across training better than unnormalized Lipschitz constants.

fits_no_version.finding: Normalized margins distinguish natural datasets, randomized labels, and randomized inputs by apparent difficulty.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Spectrally normalized margin distributions distinguish task difficulty in these AlexNet experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Normalized margin distributions converge while weight norms continue growing.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normalized margins can stabilize during training despite growing weight norms.

fits_no_version.finding: Tested l2 regularization levels produce no visible improvement in margin distributions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight decay has little visible effect on normalized margins in this AlexNet setup.

fits_no_version.finding: Uniform input noise at scale 0.15 flips predictions for 5.86% of low-margin images versus 0.04% of high-margin images.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Low-margin inputs are more susceptible to prediction changes under uniform input noise.

record.problems: The empirical comparisons are mostly displayed as figures without exact numerical values in the text. The paper says the AlexNet setup is not optimized across datasets and disables regularization except in the explicit regularization comparison. It does not establish that SGD selects large-margin predictors as a general result; the authors identify this as missing analysis.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible result rows omitted. Theoretical bound statements and cited findings are not empirical outcomes for the listed versions.

untested.parts: Architectures other than AlexNet, ImageNet, and precise numerical endpoint accuracies.
Width sweeps beyond zero training error and their test-error consequences.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Optimizer comparisons, tuning budgets, switching optimizers, and decoupled weight decay.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout and its interactions with dataset size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized training examples versus random examples and retraining.

missing.what: Explicitly extract Figure 1's zero-training-error markers for both label conditions and the corresponding held-out errors. Existing rows record the complexity correlation but omit the fit-and-generalization evidence needed for V1.
missing.locator: Figure 1 and its caption; Section 1's definition of excess risk.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not a listed original source. Its related complexity results cannot substitute for V7's specifically defined sharpness measure. Section 3.4 states that all figures use the earlier l1 correction factor; experiments with alternative correction norms reportedly differed negligibly.

versions.untested_parts: Whether architectures and recipes that fit random labels also generalize on natural labels; random-label test accuracy.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation and their effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected comparisons and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer comparisons and tuning.
Batch-size comparisons and adaptations to large-batch training.
Dropout effects and interactions with data augmentation or weight decay.

The paper measures spectral complexity and normalized margins against excess risk, but does not perturb weights by their magnitudes or compare perturbation tolerance against norm- and margin-based measures. Its reported correlation concerns a related complexity measure rather than the version's magnitude-aware sharpness measure.
Removing memorized examples and measuring resulting test accuracy.
